title: A Doctor’s Journal Entry for August 6, 1945
tagline: A doctor steps into his garden at eight in the morning — and the entry begins again in a ruined city.

overview.intro: Seth’s poem is written as the journal entry of a Hiroshima doctor on the day the atomic bomb was dropped, and it holds two times in one document: the ordinary morning before the flash, and the walk through the aftermath afterwards. The opening is deliberately domestic — a man notices the day, steps into his garden with his cats, and is interrupted by a light more powerful than the sun. What follows is the doctor’s effort to be a doctor: he makes his way towards his hospital through streets that no longer resemble streets, while the journal’s voice keeps its professional composure — who is living, who is dying, who should be attended first. Published summaries record that the entry closes as it will keep being written: the doctor, himself injured, returns home to his ruined house and takes up the pen again, because the record must continue. The poem’s restraint is its power: no rhetoric against the bomb, only a doctor’s observations in a doctor’s order. This chapter follows the two movements of the entry and reads how Seth builds horror out of precision.

learn.title: Before you read: the diary as a form of witness

blocks.text: A journal entry makes a particular promise: that the writer does not yet know what the day will hold. Seth uses that promise as the poem’s structure. The first lines belong to an ordinary day — the heat, the hour, the garden, the cats — because at eight in the morning on 6 August 1945 that is genuinely all anyone in Hiroshima knew. The reader, who does know, is therefore placed in the unbearable position of waiting for the flash inside a domestic scene, and the poem’s first lesson is about how catastrophe actually arrives: inside routine, interrupting nothing in particular. The second lesson concerns the speaker. A doctor is a trained observer — trained to look, to classify, to decide who can be helped and in what order — and Seth lets that training govern the poem’s diction after the bomb, so that the horror is reported in professional categories rather than in outcry. It is worth reading the poem alongside the documentary tradition it belongs to: survivor testimony, the atomic-bomb memoirs and the photographs of Hiroshima. Seth’s poem is that tradition in miniature, and its closing act — the doctor returning to his journal — is the tradition’s own claim: that to write the record down is the first duty that survives everything else.

items: The journal form makes the reader wait for a flash the reader already knows is coming.
The flash interrupts routine — that is how catastrophe arrives.
The speaker is a trained observer: classification replaces outcry.
The poem belongs to the tradition of survivor testimony.
The closing act of writing is testimony claiming its first duty.

learn.title: Before the flash: the ordinary morning

blocks.text: The poem opens at eight in the morning with a man behaving like any man: rising, noticing the heat of the day, and stepping outside into his garden where his cats are. Published readings stress how carefully Seth establishes the temperature of ordinariness — the hour, the small domestic gesture, the animals — because every detail of normality is a measuring instrument for what follows. There is also, in the opening, the doctor’s self-positioning: he is at home, among his own things, in the roles of householder and cat-owner rather than physician. The flash then arrives as the interruption the poem has been preparing for: a light greater than the sun, and with it the physical collapse of the house. Notice that the doctor’s first reaction is not fear but confusion — the mind reaching for the ordinary explanations — and that he thinks of his wife inside the house. This is the hinge of the poem: the moment when a morning becomes a date in history. From that point the entry stops being a diary and becomes a record, and the doctor stops being a householder and becomes what he is trained to be.

learn.title: After: the doctor through the ruined streets

blocks.text: The second movement is a walk through a city that has been remade overnight. Published summaries describe what the doctor sees and does: he makes his way towards the hospital through streets that have lost their shapes, through smoke and dust and the remains of houses; he encounters people whose clothing has been burned away and skin hanging from their bodies; he meets the injured and the dying and, with the composure of his training, begins to distinguish — this one can walk, this one cannot, this one must be attended first. Two pressures act on him simultaneously: his own wounds and the professional imperative to ignore them in favour of those who need a doctor more. The poem’s middle is therefore an argument conducted without words — duty against suffering — and the doctor’s discipline in it is the poem’s moral centre. Seth refuses spectacle at every point: the details are precise, never amplified, and the restraint makes them worse rather than better, because the reader supplies what the line declines to. By the end of the walk the doctor has failed to reach his hospital in any normal sense, and his direction turns homewards — towards the ruin of his own house and, with it, the journal he will take up again.

items: The streets have lost their shapes; landmarks are gone.
The injured appear without clothing, with skin hanging from their bodies.
The doctor classifies: who can walk, who cannot, who must be helped first.
His own injuries are subordinated to his duty — the poem’s moral centre.
Seth’s restraint: precise details, never amplified.

learn.title: The closing entry, and how the poem works

blocks.text: The poem ends where testimony begins: the doctor, himself wounded and having reached his ruined home, takes up the journal again and resumes the entry. Published readings treat the gesture as the poem’s true subject — the record continuing because the record is what remains, and because the act of writing is the last form the doctor’s duty can take when medicine has nothing left to offer. Formally, the device is a loop: the entry’s opening line returns, so that the poem reads as a document interrupted and resumed rather than a lyric with a peroration. The effect of the whole is built on three technical means. Precision over passion: exact times, exact classifications, an observer’s vocabulary — the horror is in the accuracy. Contrast: the garden and cats against the ruined street, the domestic and the historic held in one document. And the withheld judgement: the poem never denounces, never names a villain, never explains the politics, which leaves the reader to hold the outrage alone — and makes the outrage the reader’s own rather than the poem’s assertion. The result is the quality Seth seems after throughout: a witness who is also a doctor, writing because that is what doctors do when they can no longer heal.

learn.title: Themes, and preparation for the examination

blocks.text: The horror of nuclear war is the poem’s public theme, and it is conveyed entirely by the before-and-after of an ordinary morning. Duty and humanity is the private theme: the doctor’s training does not make him indifferent, it makes him useful, and the poem’s admiration is reserved for that discipline. Testimony and memory is the formal theme: a journal kept through the end of the entry asserts that events which destroy a city cannot destroy the record of it. For the examination, expect questions on the two movements and the effect of each; on how the poet creates horror (precision, contrast, restraint — answer with technique, not with the details alone); on the doctor’s character as revealed by his conduct; and on the significance of the closing. Short answers often ask for specific moments — the opening scene, the doctor’s encounter with the injured, the return home — so know the sequence. As throughout this site, the poem’s lines are not reproduced here: verify every quotation you intend to use against your own prescribed copy, and attribute it correctly.

keyPoints: The poem is a journal entry for 6 August 1945 — the day the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.
It opens at eight in the morning: heat, the garden, the cats, an ordinary domestic scene.
The flash — a light greater than the sun — interrupts the morning and collapses the house.
The doctor then walks towards his hospital through streets that have lost their shapes.
He encounters the burned and the dying, and classifies the injured by who can be helped.
His own wounds are subordinated to his duty: care ordered by need.
Seth’s method: precision over passion, contrast, and a judgement that is withheld.
The entry closes as the doctor, home and wounded, takes up the journal again.

questions.prompt: What was the doctor doing when the bomb was dropped?
options: He had stepped into his garden with his cats
He was travelling to the hospital
questions.answer: He had stepped into his garden with his cats
questions.explanation: The entry opens at eight in the morning with the doctor outside in his garden — domestic ordinariness that the flash interrupts.
questions.commonMistake: He is not yet at work; the poem begins at home.

options: A free-verse journal entry for a single date
questions.answer: A free-verse journal entry for a single date
questions.explanation: The title and structure give the poem its documentary form: an entry for 6 August 1945, written in free verse and resumed at its close.
questions.commonMistake: Do not call it a report; it is a personal journal, though it documents.

questions.prompt: What best describes the doctor’s conduct after the flash?
options: He walks towards his hospital, classifying the injured while wounded himself
He searches only for his cats
questions.answer: He walks towards his hospital, classifying the injured while wounded himself
questions.explanation: The middle of the entry is professional duty in action: ordering help by need while subordinating his own injuries.
questions.commonMistake: He does not abandon his post; the question is about duty under suffering.

questions.prompt: How does the poem primarily create its effect of horror?
options: By precise observation and restraint rather than by outcry
By denouncing the bomb in direct speeches
By describing explosions in exaggerated detail
By rhyming laments for the dead
questions.answer: By precise observation and restraint rather than by outcry
questions.explanation: The doctor reports in an observer’s categories and the poem withholds judgement, so the reader supplies the outrage — which makes it stronger.
questions.commonMistake: The poem never denounces; rhetoric would weaken its documentary authority.

questions.prompt: The journal entry is dated 6 August ______, the day the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.
questions.explanation: The date in the title is the poem’s anchor: everything in the entry is measured against that historical morning.
questions.commonMistake: The year is part of the title — keep it exact.

questions.prompt: How does the poem establish the ordinariness of the morning before the flash?
questions.answer: It gives the exact hour — eight in the morning — and a domestic scene: the heat of the day, the doctor stepping out of his house into his garden, and his cats about him. He is in the role of householder rather than physician, and nothing in the routine suggests anything other than a normal summer day, which is exactly what makes the interruption devastating.
questions.explanation: The answer must name the specific details, because each one is a measuring instrument for what follows.
questions.commonMistake: Do not describe the flash here; the question is about the establishment of normality.

questions.prompt: How does the doctor behave when he encounters the injured in the streets?
questions.answer: With professional composure: he moves through the ruined streets towards his work and begins to classify the people he meets — who can walk, who cannot, who must be attended first — ordering his help by need rather than by proximity. Even while injured himself he subordinates his own condition, since a wounded doctor is still more useful than the most severely hurt among those he can treat.
questions.explanation: Classification and self-subordination are the two acts; both belong in the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer only that he helped “everyone”; the poem’s point is ordered judgement.

questions.prompt: How does Seth use the contrast between the two parts of the journal entry?
questions.answer: The entry is built on a single contrast: the same man, the same street, one morning apart. The first part accumulates normality — the hour, the heat, the garden, the cats — and every detail is chosen so that the reader feels a life intact. The flash converts that life into a document, and the second part walks the identical ground in ruins: the house collapsed, the streets unreadable, the people burned of clothing and composure. The contrast works because nothing is explained between the halves; the poem supplies the before and the after, and the reader performs the violence in the gap. It also reorganises the speaker: the householder of the first part becomes the physician of the second, so that the human change is measured in role as well as scenery — from a man among his cats to a man who must decide who is helped first. The final reversal of the contrast comes at the very end, when the doctor returns to the ruins of his home and takes up the journal: the house is gone, but the entry continues, and the surviving half of the contrast is not the property but the record.
questions.explanation: The answer names the contrast, shows how the gap between the halves does the work, tracks the change of role, and closes on the ending’s reversal of it.
questions.commonMistake: Do not simply describe both halves; the question asks how the contrast is used.

questions.prompt: What kind of person is the doctor, according to the poem? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: He is a man whose profession has become his character. Before the flash he is domestic and unhurried — a householder in his garden — and the abruptness with which that role ends shows how little it protected him. After it, three qualities appear. Trained observation: he looks at the ruined street and reports what he sees in the categories of his work — who can walk, who cannot, who needs attention first — so that classification, for him, is a way of remaining useful. Self-subordination: wounded himself, he keeps treating others, because a doctor’s injury ranks below his patient’s need; the poem does not dramatise this as heroism, it simply records it, which is how we know it is habitual. And continuity: having reached his ruined home, he takes up the journal again, showing that the habit of record-keeping is as deep in him as the habit of care. Together these make a portrait of duty as a form of humanity — not opposed to feeling, but the shape feeling takes when a professional has trained it for thirty years.
questions.explanation: Three qualities — observation, self-subordination, continuity — each anchored in a moment of the poem, with the concluding definition of duty.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer with adjectives alone; the evidence is the conduct.

questions.prompt: The poem withholds judgement about the bomb. Discuss whether that restraint makes the poem more or less powerful as a protest.
questions.answer: The restraint is the protest, and the argument can be made on three grounds. First, authority: the poem’s speaker is a witness, and witnesses persuade by accuracy rather than by denunciation; had the entry accused anyone, it would have become an argument and lost the documentary weight that makes it believable. Second, reader-placement: because the poem refuses to tell us what to feel, we must supply the outrage ourselves, and an emotion a reader generates is always stronger than one asserted at them — the withheld judgement is an invitation to conclude. Third, ethics: atrocity described in rhetorical terms risks becoming spectacle, and Seth’s precision protects the dead from being used; the injured are classified, not paraded. A genuine counter-argument exists and should be conceded: protest without accusation can seem to leave the responsibility unassigned, and a reader looking for blame will not find it in the poem. But the answer to that is in the form itself — a journal entry is evidence, and evidence is what prosecutions are built from; the accusation, when it comes, will be made elsewhere, on the strength of records exactly like this one. The restraint therefore does not weaken the protest: it makes the poem last, and it makes the reader its author.
questions.explanation: The answer argues from authority, reader-placement and ethics, concedes the strongest counter-argument, and answers it from the poem’s documentary form.
questions.commonMistake: Do not declare “restraint is powerful” without the counter-argument; the discuss form rewards a staged case.
